A1.justification: Both PDFs describe The Prosody of Emojis and the same four experiments. The complete text, figures, tables and appendices support reliable matching despite substantial rewriting, reanalysis and relocation of material.

before.justification: v1 reports original human annotation, speech-production and perception results, including 3,153 recordings from 129 speakers and original acoustic and semantic analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experimental results and reports additional statistical analyses of prosodic variation, emoji identification and perceptual overlap.

M1.justification: The statistical modelling method is substantially expanded. v1 uses descriptive perception analyses and a frequentist acoustic-distance regression; v2 introduces Bayesian Models 1–5 for perceived variation, identification, convergence, acoustic distances and semantic ties. The pretrained feature extractors and semantic-clustering pipeline remain.

E1.justification: The same English-language corpus and four production/perception tasks are retained, including 230 base utterances, 1,595 emoji stimuli, 3,153 recordings, 645 within-speaker pairs and 49 inter-speaker pairs. Newly documented participant attributes and separate analyses of existing contrast types do not establish expanded population or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 explicitly compares joint emoji-identification accuracy against a 25% random-assignment baseline in Section 4.2, also discussing random-choice performance in Appendix B.1. v1 reports correct, incorrect and skipped proportions without this explicit chance comparison. No competing trained systems are added.

E3.justification: v2 changes the stated speech-rate metric from syllables per second to characters per second. New perception analyses introduce demographic, microphone, familiarity and contrast-type controls and a semantic-tie outcome. Experiment 4's reported average judgments per pair changes from approximately five to four; this reporting revision does not establish new data collection.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analyses of factors associated with communication success, including emoji familiarity, demographic and microphone effects, contrast types and familiarity interactions. Appendix C adds a dedicated semantic-tie analysis, while Appendix B.1 adds rank-correlation tests. The earlier qualitative cases, ambiguity examples and semantic-alignment analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1's acoustic regression reports coefficients and p-values; v2 reports Bayesian credible intervals, posterior probabilities and directional evidence ratios. Appendix A adds prior specifications and convergence reporting, including R-hat below 1.01, trace inspection and effective sample size checks. New Spearman significance tests supplement the unchanged Fisher-based confidence intervals for semantic correlations.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for the new perception and semantic-tie models and replaces v1 Table 2's acoustic estimates with posterior contrasts in Figure 4 under revised analysis settings. Inter-speaker similarity now has an estimated coefficient of 2.42 with a 95% credible interval of [1.66, 3.22]. The highest-expressivity-bin correct rate changes from 64.68% to 62.50% in the corresponding passages. Inter-speaker response percentages and semantic-alignment scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal specifications for the new statistical models, including Bernoulli likelihoods with logit links and Normal(0, 0.5) fixed-effect priors in Appendix A. These extend the mathematical assumptions beyond v1's acoustic mixed-effects formula. Neither version presents theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The four central research questions and the claimed connection between emoji semantics and prosody remain. v2 adds explicit above-chance identification claims and identifies intensity and timing as primary acoustic carriers in the conclusion. These refine and strengthen particular claims within the existing contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations involving digital fluency, semantic conflict, same-category emojis as prosodic stabilisers, and pitch-tracking fragility. Its new Limitations section addresses elicited versus spontaneous speech, dialect coverage, the small listener sample, acoustic-proxy validity, stimulus selection and emoji rendering. These substantially expand v1's discussion of ambiguity and expressive variability.

D1.justification: v2 adds a Hugging Face dataset location, R/brms/Stan implementation information, priors, convergence checks, transformation details, listener counts, demographic variables and microphone categories. However, it removes v1's precise YouTube collection dates and procedure, spaCy filtering description, Whisper Medium specification, 20% word-error threshold and detailed recording-exclusion rules. Reproducibility documentation therefore gains important information while losing other specifics.

R1.justification: The background adds connections to punctuation and typography through Drury et al. and de Lacerda Pataca and Costa, alongside psychological and Bayesian references. Several earlier emotion-interpretation and preprocessing citations disappear. The central positioning as an empirical study of human emoji-influenced speech remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, background, methods, results, discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Statistical analysis receives a dedicated methods subsection; Qualitative Analysis becomes Discussion; descriptive results move into Appendix B; and model specifications, perceptual-overlap analysis, limitations and ethics sections are added. Earlier Appendices A–D largely map to later Appendices D–G.

P2.justification: v2 adds regression Tables 1, 2 and 5 and replaces the earlier acoustic coefficient/p-value table with a three-panel forest plot. Figure 1 moves from a full-width display to the first-page column with recoloured intensity curves. The listener-accuracy plot and inter-speaker table move to the appendix, and the earlier semantic-contrast schematic disappears. Clustering, correlation and interface displays are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 makes previously descriptive listener findings more assessable through explicit statistical models and uncertainty, adds a useful perceptual-overlap analysis, and documents limitations and a dataset location. The gain is limited by removal of corpus/filter details and some overstated interpretations, including describing the approximately 11-fold odds ratio in Section 4.3 as being '11 times more likely'. Overall, the added analytical transparency supports a limited net improvement.
